title: Binet's Formula and Lamé's 5-Digit Bound
description: Proves Lamé's 5-digit bound without restriction (euclideanSteps(a,b) ≤ 5·decimalDigits(b) for all b > 0) and Binet's formula fib(n) = (φⁿ - ψⁿ)/√5. Part I: the five-step Fibonacci identity fib(5k+7) ≥ 10·fib(5k+2) implies fib(5k+2) ≥ 10^k. Part II: Binet's formula via paired induction, with φ⁵ > 10 explaining why 5 digits correspond to one Euclidean step. 21 theorems, 2 definitions, 0 axioms.

meta.author: Lean Genius
meta.assumptions: None. Fully machine-verified. Depends on GCDAlgorithmOQ01 (euclideanSteps, decimalDigits, lame_step_bound).
originalContributions: fib_ge_pow10_general: fib(5k+2) ≥ 10^k for all k (no restriction)
binet_formula: fib(n) = (φⁿ - ψⁿ)/√5 proved by paired induction
phi_pow5_gt_10: φ⁵ > 10, explaining why 5 digits correspond to one GCD step

overview.historicalContext: Gabriel Lamé's 1844 paper presented to the French Academy is historically the first rigorous analysis of algorithm complexity, predating the modern theory of computation by a century. Lamé proved that the Euclidean algorithm on $b$ requires at most $5 \cdot \lfloor \log_{10} b \rfloor + 1$ steps — the first result bounding an algorithm's runtime by a property of its input size. The constant 5 is explained by Jacques Philippe Marie Binet's 1843 formula $F_n = (\varphi^n - \psi^n)/\sqrt{5}$, where $\varphi = (1+\sqrt{5})/2$ is the golden ratio: since $\varphi^5 \approx 11.09 > 10$, every 5 Fibonacci steps multiplies the value by a factor exceeding 10, consuming one decimal digit. The golden ratio itself was known to Euclid (Elements, Book VI), who described it as the "extreme and mean ratio"; the formula connecting it to Fibonacci numbers appears to have been known to Albert Girard (1634) and rediscovered by Binet.
overview.problemStatement: Prove (1) $F_{5k+2} \geq 10^k$ for all $k \geq 0$ (no restriction on $k$), giving the unrestricted Lamé bound $\text{euclideanSteps}(a,b) \leq 5 \cdot \text{decimalDigits}(b)$; (2) Binet's formula $F_n = (\varphi^n - \psi^n)/\sqrt{5}$; (3) $\varphi^5 > 10$, the golden ratio explanation for why 5 decimal digits correspond to one Euclidean step.
overview.text:
**Part I**: The five-step identity $F_{n+5} = 5F_{n+1} + 3F_n$ (from four Fibonacci recurrences, closed by omega) implies $F_{5k+7} \geq 10 \cdot F_{5k+2}$. By induction, $F_{5k+2} \geq 10^k$. Since $b < 10^{d+1} \leq F_{5(d+1)+2}$ where $d = \lfloor \log_{10} b \rfloor$, the parent module's `lame_step_bound` yields the result.

**Part II** (Binet namespace): $\varphi = (1+\sqrt{5})/2$, $\psi = (1-\sqrt{5})/2$ satisfy $\varphi^2 = \varphi+1$ and $\psi^2 = \psi+1$ (both roots of $x^2-x-1=0$). Binet's formula is proved by paired induction: simultaneously prove the formula for $F_n$ and $F_{n+1}$; the recurrence step uses $\varphi^2 = \varphi+1$ to reduce $\varphi^{n+2}$ to $\varphi^n$ and $\varphi^{n+1}$. Consequences: $|\psi| < 1$ ($\psi \to 0$), nearest integer property, and $\varphi^5 = 5\varphi+3 > 10$.
overview.proofStrategy:
**Part I**: `fib_add_five` by linear arithmetic from four Fibonacci recurrences. `fib_five_step_growth` by omega after unfolding 5 Fibonacci values. `fib_ge_pow10_general` by induction using `fib_five_step_growth`. Generalized Lamé by connecting to `lame_step_bound` from parent module via `Nat.log`.

**Part II**: `phi_sq`/`psi_sq` by `ring_nf` + `Real.sq_sqrt`. `binet_pair` by paired induction; inductive step uses exponent factoring (`e1`/`e2`), `phi_sq`/`psi_sq`, and `ring`. `phi_pow5_gt_10` by computing $\varphi^5 = 5\varphi+3$ and bounding $\varphi > 7/5$ from $\sqrt{5} > 9/5$.
keyInsights: Five-step growth $F_{5k+7} \geq 10 \cdot F_{5k+2}$ is the direct arithmetic explanation of '5 digits' — this elementary identity suffices for the bound without any mention of the golden ratio.

Binet's formula shows $F_n = \text{round}(\varphi^n/\sqrt{5})$, the nearest integer to $\varphi^n/\sqrt{5}$ — a remarkable bridge between the discrete Fibonacci sequence and continuous exponential growth.
$\varphi^5 > 10$: each 5 Fibonacci steps multiplies by more than 10, consuming one decimal digit — this is the golden ratio's geometric explanation for the constant 5 in Lamé's theorem.
$|\psi| < 1$: the conjugate root $\psi \approx -0.618$ contributes only exponentially vanishing corrections $\psi^n/\sqrt{5}$ — this is why the formula gives integers despite involving $\sqrt{5}$.

The proof naturally separates into two complementary views: Part I is a self-contained elementary proof (no real numbers needed), while Part II provides the deeper structural explanation via the characteristic equation $x^2 - x - 1 = 0$ and its roots in $\mathbb{R}$.

conclusion.summary: Machine-verifies both the unrestricted Lamé 5-digit bound ($\text{euclideanSteps}(a,b) \leq 5 \cdot \text{decimalDigits}(b)$ for all $b > 0$) and Binet's formula ($F_n = (\varphi^n - \psi^n)/\sqrt{5}$), with the key insight $\varphi^5 > 10$ connecting them. 21 theorems, 2 definitions, 0 axioms, 280 lines.
conclusion.implications: This proof sits at the intersection of three deep ideas: algorithm complexity analysis, the Fibonacci sequence, and the golden ratio. The fact that Lamé's 1844 complexity bound can be explained both elementarily (five-step growth identity) and via transcendental algebra (Binet's formula) illustrates a recurrent theme in mathematics: elementary arguments often have deeper structural explanations. The golden ratio $\varphi$ appears here as the spectral radius of the Fibonacci recurrence matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, whose eigenvalues are precisely $\varphi$ and $\psi$. The formalization demonstrates that both views — discrete induction and continuous exponential analysis — can coexist rigorously in Lean 4.
openQuestions: Can the tight worst case be formalized: the Euclidean algorithm on $(F_{n+1}, F_n)$ requires exactly $n-1$ steps, showing Lamé's bound is sharp?
Prove Zeckendorf's theorem: every positive integer has a unique representation as a sum of non-consecutive Fibonacci numbers (Zeckendorf, 1972).

Can the matrix diagonalization proof of Binet's formula ($\begin{pmatrix}F_{n+1}\\F_n\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}^n \begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}$) be formalized in Mathlib?

sections.title: Imports and Module Overview
sections.summary: Imports GCDAlgorithmOQ01 (parent module with euclideanSteps, decimalDigits, lame_step_bound) and Mathlib. The docstring explains the two-part structure: Part I removes the 10^20 restriction via elementary Fibonacci arithmetic; Part II proves Binet's formula and the golden ratio connection.

sections.title: Five-Step Fibonacci Identity
sections.summary: fib_add_five: fib(n+5) = 5·fib(n+1) + 3·fib(n), proved by unfolding four Fibonacci recurrences and closing with omega. The linear combination 5·fib(n+1)+3·fib(n) is the exact closed form for fib(n+5) and is the foundation for the multiplicative growth estimate.

sections.title: Multiplicative Growth: fib(5k+7) ≥ 10·fib(5k+2)
sections.summary: fib_five_step_growth: proves fib(5k+7) ≥ 10·fib(5k+2) by expanding all intermediate values (fib(5k+2) through fib(5k+7)) via fib_add_two, using Nat.fib_mono for fib(5k) ≤ fib(5k+1), then closing with omega. This is the key multiplicative step used in the inductive proof.

sections.title: Main Bound: fib(5k+2) ≥ 10^k for All k
sections.summary: fib_ge_pow10_general: induction on k. Base case fib(2)=1≥1 by simp. Inductive step: 10^(k+1) = 10·10^k ≤ 10·fib(5k+2) ≤ fib(5k+7) = fib(5(k+1)+2). The calc block chains these inequalities cleanly using the multiplicative growth lemma.

sections.title: Generalized Lamé 5-Digit Bound
sections.summary: lame_five_digit_bound_general: connects fib_ge_pow10_general to the parent module's lame_step_bound. Uses Nat.log 10 b = d, then Nat.lt_pow_succ_log_self for b < 10^(d+1) ≤ fib(5(d+1)+2). Two native_decide examples verify concrete cases.

sections.title: Golden Ratio Definitions (Binet Namespace)
sections.summary: Opens the Binet namespace with two noncomputable definitions: goldenPhi = (1+√5)/2 ≈ 1.618 and goldenPsi = (1-√5)/2 ≈ -0.618. Both are the roots of x²-x-1=0, the characteristic polynomial of the Fibonacci recurrence.

sections.title: Algebraic Properties of φ, ψ, and √5
sections.summary: Proves: sqrt5_pos, sqrt5_sq (√5·√5=5), sqrt5_gt_two (√5>2), phi_sub_psi (φ-ψ=√5), phi_add_psi (φ+ψ=1, Vieta sum), phi_mul_psi (φψ=-1, Vieta product), phi_sq (φ²=φ+1), psi_sq (ψ²=ψ+1), phi_pos (φ>0). These are proved by ring_nf + Real.sq_sqrt.

sections.title: Binet's Formula Proof by Paired Induction
sections.summary: binet_pair proves simultaneously F(n)=(φⁿ-ψⁿ)/√5 and F(n+1)=(φⁿ⁺¹-ψⁿ⁺¹)/√5 by induction. Base: F(0)=0=(1-1)/√5; F(1)=1=(φ-ψ)/√5=√5/√5. Step: F(n+2)=F(n)+F(n+1), then use φⁿ⁺²=φⁿ·φ²=φⁿ·(φ+1) and similarly for ψ. binet_formula extracts the first component.

sections.title: Consequences: |ψ| < 1 and Nearest Integer Property
sections.summary: abs_psi_lt_one: |ψ| < 1 from ψ∈(-1,0) (using √5<3 for upper bound, √5>1 for lower). fib_nearest_integer: |F(n) - φⁿ/√5| < 1/2, i.e., fib(n) is the nearest integer to φⁿ/√5. Proved by binet_formula + |ψ|^n/√5 ≤ 1/√5 < 1/2.

sections.title: φ⁵ > 10: The Golden Ratio Explanation
sections.summary: Computes φ³=2φ+1, φ⁴=3φ+2, φ⁵=5φ+3 by iterating φ²=φ+1. Then phi_pow5_gt_10 bounds φ>7/5 from √5>9/5 (via sqrt5_sq and nlinarith), giving φ⁵=5φ+3>7+3=10. Ends with three binet_formula verification examples (n=0,1,10).
